opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a pretty dramatic shift for me personally. Up until maybe last fall, my workflow was mostly autocomplete. I'd be in the editor writing code, the model would suggest the next few lines, I'd tab through, and I was still very much the one driving. Somewhere around December, with the newer models and the agentic tooling around them, it kind of flipped. Now I'm mostly describing what I want in English, the agent goes off and writes big chunks of code, runs things, fixes its own errors, and I'm reviewing diffs. I went from something like 80% writing code myself to maybe 80% delegating, and that happened over a few weeks, which is kind of wild for a habit I've had for twenty years.

It's not all roses, though. The agents are incredibly capable in some ways and surprisingly dumb in others. They'll write a few hundred lines that mostly work, then make a subtle conceptual mistake, or overcomplicate something that should be ten lines, or confidently make assumptions without checking with you. So I've had to learn a new skill of supervising them: keeping them on a short leash, giving them small, well-scoped tasks, reading what they produce, and stepping in when they go off the rails. It feels less like programming and more like managing a very fast, very eager intern with jagged abilities.

I'll also say it's changed how I feel about coding. There's a bit of atrophy. I notice I'm less fluent at writing certain things from scratch because I just don't anymore. But the leverage is huge, and I've been building things I wouldn't have bothered with before because the activation energy was too high. So overall it's net very positive, but I think we're all still figuring out the right workflows, and the tooling is changing so fast that whatever I'm doing today probably looks different in three months.

r001.rationale: The response describes delegating code to agents and increased leverage, but does not identify typing speed as a bottleneck that coding agents relax.

r002.rationale: It describes a shift around December from writing code mostly himself to delegating roughly 80% of the work to agents.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss whether the general public appreciates the magnitude of the workflow change.

r004.rationale: It does not raise how to scale agent use beyond a single session.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so December was kind of a dividing line for me personally. Before that, I was mostly in what I'd call the autocomplete era, and then maybe the chat era, where you're copy-pasting snippets back and forth and you're still very much the one holding the keyboard. The agent stuff flipped that. Suddenly I'm not writing code so much as I'm supervising something that writes code, and that's a very different cognitive mode.

The honest version is that it was uncomfortable at first. I've been programming for a long time, and there's a muscle memory to it, a sense of ownership over every line. With agents you have to let go of that. You describe the thing, you go get coffee, you come back, and there's a diff. And the diff is often really good. Sometimes it's subtly wrong in a way that takes me longer to find than it would have taken to just write it. So the skill that got rewarded changed. It became less about typing and more about specifying clearly, decomposing the problem well, and then being a very good reviewer.

I also noticed my own output went up a lot, but in a lopsided way. The boring stuff, the glue code, the test scaffolding, the little scripts, that basically became free. The hard stuff, the part where you actually need to think about the architecture or have a real insight about the problem, that's still mine. The agent doesn't really do that part yet. So the shape of a day changed. More thinking, less typing, a lot more reading.

And then there's this weird thing where you start to anthropomorphize the agent a little. You develop intuitions about what it's good at, when it's going to go off the rails, when you need to step in. It's a bit like managing a very fast, very eager junior engineer who has read everything but has no taste yet. You learn to give it guardrails. You learn to keep the loop tight. I think a lot of the people who struggled with it early were trying to give it enormous tasks and then being disappointed. The ones who did well figured out the right granularity.

So overall, I'd say it's the biggest change in how I actually work since I started. Not because the models got dramatically smarter overnight, but because the interface finally matched what the models could already do.

r001.rationale: The response says output increased and work shifted from typing to thinking and reviewing, but it does not identify typing speed as a bottleneck on individual accomplishment.

r002.rationale: It describes December as a dividing line, shifting from writing code himself to supervising an agent that writes it.

r003.rationale: It calls the change the biggest in how he works, but does not say the general public underestimates the magnitude of the workflow change.

r004.rationale: It discusses task granularity and managing an agent, but does not raise how to scale personal agent use beyond a single session.

astra-6.text:
I think the big shift is that you’re going from writing the code yourself, with an assistant helping you along, to delegating a task and reviewing what comes back. And that sounds like a small change, but it’s a very different way of working.

With autocomplete, you’re still driving. You know what file you’re in, you know what you’re trying to do, and the model fills in a few lines. With an agent, you can say, “Here’s the behavior I want,” and it can go look through the repository, make changes, run tests, and iterate. You’re moving up a level of abstraction.

But then the bottleneck shifts. Can you specify the task clearly? Can you tell whether the implementation is actually correct? Passing tests is useful, but it doesn’t necessarily mean the agent solved the problem you intended. So you have this interesting situation where generating code gets much cheaper, but having good judgment about code becomes more important.

And I think we’re still figuring out the workflow. When do you let it run? When do you intervene? How do you give it enough context without micromanaging it? That feels like a new skill, and the capabilities are changing fast enough that you have to keep recalibrating.

r001.rationale: It says code generation is getting cheaper, but does not identify typing speed as a bottleneck that coding agents relax.

r002.rationale: It describes moving from writing code yourself with assistance to delegating tasks to an agent and reviewing the results; the preceding question supplies the December timeframe.

r003.rationale: It does not say that the general public underestimates the magnitude of the workflow change.

r004.rationale: It discusses managing an agent within a workflow, but does not raise scaling personal use beyond a single agent session.

sol-6.1.text:
The big shift for me is that I’m spending less time writing the code directly and more time describing what I want, letting an agent take a pass, and then inspecting the result. And that changes the feel of programming quite a bit. You’re still responsible for the software, but you’re working at a different level of abstraction.

The tricky part is calibrating how much to delegate. Sometimes you can hand over a fairly substantial task and it just works, and sometimes something that looks simple turns into a lot of back-and-forth. So you’re constantly developing this intuition for where the models are capable and where you need to stay very involved.

I think that’s the interesting transition: the bottleneck starts moving from producing code to specifying the right thing and verifying that you actually got it. You can generate a lot more software, but you still have to understand what you’re building.

r001.rationale: It says the bottleneck is shifting from producing code to specifying and verifying, but does not identify typing speed as the bottleneck being relaxed.

r003.rationale: It discusses changes in programming workflow but does not say the general public underestimates the magnitude of that change.

r004.rationale: It discusses calibrating delegation to agents, but does not raise scaling personal use beyond a single agent session.
